title: Merseyside's most haunted and spookiest pubs
excerpt: As a city with a rich and varied history, it's no surprise many spots become hotbeds for supposed paranormal activity

Merseyside’s most haunted pubs and the chilling tales behind them

As a city with a rich and varied history, it's no surprise many spots become hotbeds for supposed paranormal activity

18:56, 31 Oct 2026

Liverpool’s pubs are known for their history, character and lively atmosphere, but some are said to have a few unexpected regulars.

‌

‌

From a centuries-old watering hole where the ghost of a murdered sailor is said to linger to a city-centre pub with tales of a mischievous spirit summoned during a séance, Liverpool has no shortage of eerie stories attached to its drinking establishments. Some claim to have seen unexplained figures, while others tell of strange sounds and unsettling encounters that have become part of local folklore.

‌

To mark Halloween, the ECHO has taken a look inside some of Liverpool’s most haunted pubs and the ghost stories that have helped give them their spooky reputations.

‌

Ye Hole in Ye Wall

Ye Hole in Ye Wall is located on Hackins Hey on an ancient Quaker graveyard and dates back to 1726, making it Liverpool’s oldest pub.

The ECHO previously reported how the city centre tavern has seen a number of ghostly occurrences since landlord Stephen Hoy took it over in 2000. The most common ghoulish sighting by staff and customers is an eerie figure in a long wax jacket who has often been spotted lingering in the bar.

‌

This haunting spectre has often been confused for one of the regulars by staff, and even been spotted heading upstairs to the cellar. The ghostly sighting is reportedly an old sailor who wears a long wax coat.

It was reported that spooky encounters include elastic bands flying across the bar, lights fusing while staff are working in the cellar, and a glowing orb caught levitating over the bar on CCTV.

‌

Peter Kavanagh’s

Based in the Georgian Quarter, Peter Kavanagh's is one of the city's longest-running and most beloved pubs.

‌

But despite its status as a firm favourite spot to pull up a pew, some people believe the bar could be haunted.

A team of ghost hunters captured the moment a music box "moved by itself" while on the hunt for paranormal activity in the popular pub.

‌

The team, consisting of Chris Cummings and Adam Billing, said the movement of the music box was not a slight vibration, it was a movement over a period of about 20 seconds. They claimed there was no other explanation other than poltergeist activity.

One of the most intriguing tales centres on a séance said to have taken place around 1844. According to Tom Slemen’s Haunted Liverpool Pubs book, a spirit named Marmaduke allegedly broke out of the séance circle and is believed to have remained connected to the pub ever since, using drinkers and staff as unsuspecting mouthpieces.

‌

The Cambridge

Based on Mulberry Street, the Cambridge pub features two very different spirits in its folklore: a woman said to scratch men’s cheeks after being abandoned by her lover, and a kilted Scotsman who supposedly walks through a nearby tunnel playing bagpipes and is a sign of impending bad news.

In his book Haunted Liverpool Pubs, Tom Slemen said: "No one knows her identity, but a medium claimed the sadistic spook is the ghost of a woman who was deserted by a lover at the pub many years ago in the 1930s.

‌

"The other ghost is that of the so-called Subterranean Scotsman - a kilted ghost who is said to walk through a tunnel that comes near to the pub playing bagpipes; to hear him is a sign of approaching bad news."

‌

The Slaughter House

Considered one of Liverpool's oldest pubs, the venue on Fenwick Street is believed to have opened around 1723.

‌

Whether it is glasses randomly smashing or a mysterious shadow going into the toilets, there have been countless ghoulish tales in the Slaughter House over the years.

The pub's haunted history includes the tale of a young child having being killed in the basement, and visitors have reported seeing a shadowy figure staring at people.

‌

Back in 2017, TV show Most Haunted paid a visit and said this figure was believed to be a man called Albert. According to host Yvette Fielding, Albert “looked after horses” and may have been pushed down The Slaughter House stairs.

The Old Post Office

‌

One of the darker stories attached to Liverpool’s pubs centres on a supposedly sealed upstairs room and a mysterious presence described in local lore as a “nameless terror”.

In 1902, the little pub on School Lane in the city centre was being run by a 50-year-old Staffordshire man named Thomas Henshaw, along with his 46-year-old wife Annie, who hailed from North Wales.

‌

When the Henshaws took over the pub, they discovered a little room upstairs that was locked, and its keyhole was plugged with putty.

There was a rumour the room should never be opened as it contained a terrifying spirit. But an old friend of Mrs Henshaw, staying at the pub one night, unblocked the keyhole and peeped in at something which is claimed to have turned his mind and left him foaming at the mouth.

‌

The Bridewell

Housed in a former Victorian police lock-up, the Bridewell has an obvious atmospheric advantage. Accounts of its hauntings include a female presence associated with the old cells. The building's former use gives you a strong historical introduction even before the ghost story begins.

‌

The Magazine Hotel

The Magazine Hotel is a historic pub in New Brighton, built in 1759, widely associated with local ghost stories and folklore.

‌

Tales of the supernatural have swirled around the pub for decades. The pub’s most famous ghost story is that of a Liscard woman tortured and drowned in the Mersey during the witch hunts of the 17th century, which landlords have witnessed in the upstairs living quarters.

The pub is also shrouded in superstition, as it was almost destroyed in a blaze after a customer stole its witch.

‌

Witch figures still hang above the bar, replacing an old felt witch doll that was placed above the bar for more than a century.

Generations of staff and regulars were warned not to touch the witch figure, with a history of accidents befalling those who failed to heed the warning. When the pub suffered £200,000 worth of damage in a devastating blaze in 2010, the then-managers Linda and Les Baxendale believed the witch’s curse was to blame.

‌

The blaze, started by a power surge which blew up the pub's fuse box, left the Baxendales living in a caravan for three months while the pub was restored to its former glory.

‌

Linda told the ECHO at the time: “Part of the history of the pub is the two witches and a little devil, all made from brown felt, which were hanging by the bar.

“No-one knows exactly how long they were there, and we don't know who gave them to the pub, but we think they were there for at least 100 years.

‌

“They were covered in cobwebs and dust because we were told that if anyone touched them, bad things would happen to them.”

When the couple took over the pub in 2000 the Baxendales received an anonymous call warning them not to touch the witches. But Linda said a man was seen to take one of the figures from the ceiling two days before the blaze.

Linda added: "I suppose I am superstitious, because I used to say to the witches, 'I tell people not to touch you, so look after me'. When I found out one had gone, I said, 'Something bad is going to happen now'."
